docs.title: Build an improvement loop
docs.text:
Choose what you want to improve. Each recipe names the candidate, its fixed evaluation, and the runnable example. Start with meeting notes → action items if you are new to the API.

Improve a reusable prompt

I want to improve… What changes What measures it Recipe A prompt Instructions Generated responses across cases Prompt improvement Code Source files Independent tests Source repair An agent's skills Skill documents Agent behavior on tasks Skill libraries An agent harness Allowed harness surfaces Bounded task episodes Harness evolution Search itself Policy artifacts Inner improvement-run outcomes Policy evolution A research procedure Declared procedure Its experimental outcomes Autoresearch

docs.title: Keep the evaluation boundary visible
docs.text:
A proposer can change the artifact, not its evaluator, permissions, outer budget, or promotion rule. Development scores and feedback guide selection. Private answers are still part of development if their scores influence that selection. Only a separate final evaluation checks performance outside it.

The meeting-notes, harness, policy, and research-procedure examples include separate final checks. Source repair and support-ticket routing do not have an untouched split. The skill-library recipe identifies the different boundaries of its two variants. Every offline result remains evidence about a fixture.

To adapt a recipe, replace its model/proposer boundary and evaluation cases explicitly. Keep the other components fixed while checking that change. The complete catalog lists commands and setup; the SDK guide explains user-owned calls and reported usage.

Concepts connects the examples to meta-evolution. Nested evaluation explains how to measure a procedure by executing it.

docs.title: Research and Systems References
docs.text:
This is a working map of neighboring ideas. Meta-Evolve should implement, compose, and compare these approaches rather than rename one of them as a universal solution. For a plain-language comparison with AlphaEvolve and GEPA's optimize_anything, see How Meta-Evolve compares.

Claims about capabilities in these papers belong to the cited systems. Their inclusion here does not mean Meta-Evolve has reproduced their results.

docs.title: Experience Graphs / Trellis
docs.text:
Experience Graphs: The Data Foundation for Self-Improving Agents treats the causal state produced by long-horizon search—attempts, executable artifacts, prompts, tool outputs, rewards, siblings, search statistics, and lineage—as governed database state.

Important implications for Meta-Evolve:

  • stateless agents can recover and collaborate through durable shared experience;
  • online search, causal traversal, semantic reuse, temporal reconstruction, observability, and training views operate over one logical model;
  • the system must preserve the state observed when a decision was made, not only final mutated search statistics;
  • experience retrieval is a policy with an exploration-versus-anchoring tradeoff;
  • derived skills and training views inherit provenance and access constraints.

The paper reports preliminary domain-specific results for cross-session reuse in kernel optimization, including faster early convergence and fewer buggy nodes, while aggressive reuse reduced strategy diversity and missed the best final candidate. This motivates controlled context-policy experiments rather than a general claim that more memory always improves search.

Trellis overlaps with Meta-Evolve's data plane, not its entire product scope. Meta-Evolve focuses additionally on programmable harness and search abstractions, execution adapters, contributed agents/evaluators/compute, verification, and federation.

docs.title: DSPy
docs.text:
DSPy provides a declarative programming model for modular LM programs and optimizers that compile prompts and demonstrations against metrics.

Meta-Evolve should integrate DSPy in both directions:

  • wrap a DSPy program as a versioned harness component;
  • use a DSPy optimizer for an inner prompt/program compilation loop;
  • expose Meta-Evolve examples and evaluators as DSPy-compatible data and metrics;
  • capture compiled programs as immutable artifacts;
  • let an outer Meta-Evolve policy compare DSPy with other optimizers.

The boundary is: DSPy programs LM pipelines; Meta-Evolve programs and evolves populations of executable systems, including DSPy pipelines.

docs.title: GEPA
docs.text: GEPA uses reflective textual mutation and Pareto selection to optimize LM components from task feedback. It is a reference for TextArtifact mutation, evidence-aware reflection, and Pareto retention.

docs.title: Feedback Descent
docs.text: Feedback Descent motivates structured comparison feedback followed by feedback-derived prompt edits. The research lab isolates that mechanism without claiming to reproduce its results.

docs.title: AutoData
docs.text: AutoData motivates evolving data-generation recipes with solver-based quality signals. The local lab's same-model/different-context restricted/informed setup is explicitly a teaching simplification and confounder.

docs.title: EvoSkill
docs.text: EvoSkill motivates failure-driven discovery, consolidation, and held-out selection of reusable skills. Meta-Evolve expresses this as evolution of a shipped meta.SkillSet — one skills/<name>.md document per skill — rather than a special memory subsystem. examples/research/context_evolution demonstrates the representation; its README states per mechanism what it runs and what it omits — failure-driven discovery and a held-out selection split are among the omissions. It does not reproduce the paper's system, benchmarks, or reported gains.

docs.title: ACE
docs.text: Agentic Context Engineering motivates treating the context itself as the evolving artifact: incremental generation, reflection on execution feedback, curation of individual entries, and explicit consolidation, rather than rewriting one monolithic prompt. Meta-Evolve expresses this as a meta.Text artifact holding canonical, validated JSON whose items carry stable logical identities, so an entry can be amended or retired without losing its history. examples/research/context_evolution demonstrates all four deterministically, with a model-free reflector and curator; its README states that and the rest of the omissions per mechanism. It does not reproduce the paper's system, benchmarks, transfer results, or reported gains, and claims no cross-task transfer.

docs.title: Meta-Harness
docs.text:
Meta-Harness moves optimization beyond prompts to the source code and control logic surrounding a fixed model. It motivates HarnessArtifact, typed mutation surfaces, full execution history, and external authority boundaries.

Its agentic proposer can selectively inspect the source, scores, and execution traces of prior candidates through a filesystem instead of receiving only compressed feedback. Meta-Evolve preserves this agent-directed exploration as a scoped ExperienceReader capability alongside policy-pushed context, and examples/research/harness_evolution demonstrates it — as a mechanism, and only for one artifact type. A fixed evaluator publishes each evaluated harness's complete mutable surface values as a canonical three-file value indexed in its own evidence, and the trusted adapter opens exactly the offsets that index names, under a declared operation, result, record, and character budget that fails closed. There is no filesystem: nothing is mounted, no path is browsed, and no Git history is presented. A read-only filesystem projection for coding agents, and structured graph tools adding causal traversal, logical-time queries, and governance, remain future work. Meta-Evolve does not reproduce Meta-Harness's system, benchmarks, or reported gains.

docs.title: Self-Harness
docs.text:
Self-Harness closes the loop Meta-Harness opens: an agent improves its own harness through three iterative stages — weakness mining over execution traces, proposal of diverse but minimal harness edits, and validation that accepts an edit only after regression testing. It reports relative gains of up to 132% across nine model/benchmark combinations on Terminal-Bench-2.0, SWE-bench Verified, and AppWorld, and observes that effective harness design is itself model-specific.

examples/research/harness_evolution demonstrates the weakness-mining stage only, and only as a mechanism. A fixed development evaluator publishes harness-diagnosis/v1 evidence — verifier-grounded failure clusters, the invariants already passing, and one digest per declared surface — and a deterministic context policy projects every prior attempt, including the rejected and failed ones, from those committed records. Digests, not surface values: naming which surface an earlier attempt changed is a diagnosis fact, while reading what it changed it to is the separate audited-source concern the Meta-Harness note above describes — a pull the proposer makes through the audited reader, not a wider push.

Three properties are Meta-Evolve's stricter translation, not the paper's requirements: an attempt that does not fit the declared bounds makes the bundle refuse rather than silently omit it, the proposer returns a typed unrankable failure instead of a low score, and private and held-out facts are excluded by construction because held-out evaluations publish no diagnosis at all.

This does not reproduce Self-Harness's system, benchmarks, or reported gains. It runs a model-free fixture over two repair episodes, mines weaknesses from one fixed verifier, and claims no cross-model or cross-task transfer.

docs.title: AHE
docs.text:
Agentic Harness Engineering attacks the same loop from the observability side, through three matched pillars: component observability gives every editable harness component a file-level representation so the action space is explicit and revertible; experience observability distills raw trajectories into a layered, drill-down evidence corpus an evolving agent can actually consume; and decision observability pairs every edit with a self-declared prediction, verified in the next round against task-level outcomes. Ten iterations lift pass@1 on Terminal-Bench 2 from 69.7% to 77.0%, and its ablations localize the gain to tools, middleware, and long-term memory rather than the system prompt — which the authors read as factual harness structure transferring where prose-level strategy does not.

examples/research/harness_evolution translates the third pillar. Every proposal returns a closed manifest: the authorized observations it cites, one declared surface and its value, the development behavior the edit predicts will improve, and the regressions it puts at risk. The paper's manifest also carries an inferred root cause, and its loop intersects each prediction with the next round's task-level deltas to produce a per-edit verdict and roll back the edits that fail. This example does neither; a prediction here is recorded and auditable, not yet adjudicated.

Three properties are Meta-Evolve's stricter translation, not the paper's requirements: citations resolve only against an ordered ledger of observations the trusted adapter itself authorized, so a model-written identifier is never a derivation; exactly one surface may change per proposal; and a manifest that cannot state all five fields is a typed unrankable refusal rather than a low score.

This does not reproduce AHE's system, benchmarks, transfer results, or reported gains. It runs a model-free fixture over two repair episodes, evolves two declared surfaces rather than a file tree, and claims no cross-model, cross-benchmark, or cross-family transfer.

docs.title: Shepherd
docs.text:
Shepherd is a runtime substrate that records an agent's model actions, tool calls, and environment changes as a reversible, forkable execution trace. Its unit of control is an execution in progress; Meta-Evolve's unit of evolution is an immutable artifact evaluated between trials. The two models are therefore adjacent rather than interchangeable.

A useful composition would keep Meta-Evolve in charge of tasks, search, budgets, independent evaluation, lineage, and promotion while a user-owned Shepherd-backed proposer supplies isolated execution, retained workspace output, and trace-level evidence. Any such integration should begin as an external adapter experiment: the captured artifact remains durable truth, trace references are supporting evidence, and restored or forked execution must not bypass trial or usage accounting. Shepherd's visual-artifact notebooks are also a useful teaching reference for deterministic-first examples, optional live runs, and progressive disclosure of execution internals.

docs.title: Asari inference-stack optimization
docs.text:
Asari's inference-optimization report describes many agents improving a pinned vLLM serving stack through a discover/build, evaluate, verify, and self-improve loop. It reports changes across kernels, schedulers, load balancing, and configuration, using hierarchical performance benchmarks, measurement-noise controls, and token-distribution correctness checks.

A bounded Meta-Evolve version maps cleanly onto current seams:

  • a small SourceTree overlay holds candidate kernel and configuration edits;
  • a user-owned SDK proposer investigates and changes that overlay;
  • a custom evaluator builds it against an evaluator-owned base, verifies model behavior, and returns performance metrics, uncertainty, evidence, and usage;
  • context or audited experience exposes earlier profiler and failure evidence;
  • search retains alternatives while lineage records which evidence informed each change; and
  • an external decision, never the candidate, owns production promotion.

The shipped CommandEvaluator is only a binary, single-metric exit-code adapter, so a trustworthy experiment needs a domain evaluator that parses repeated benchmark samples. A local sequential precursor is feasible, but a whole-stack implementation also needs typed mutation surfaces and portable episodes from M8 and M9, plus trusted parallel GPU workers from M11. Cross-run knowledge transfer must be introduced explicitly rather than silently widening M3's same-run experience boundary.

Meta-Evolve does not reproduce Asari's results. The scoped future work is tracked in issue #118: start with one kernel on one trusted GPU, preserve null and negative results, and defer many-agent whole-stack optimization until its dependencies ship.

docs.title: Recursive self-improvement survey
docs.text: The Last AI Built by Humans surveys execution, strategy, experience acquisition, deployment adaptation, and meta-improvement autonomy. It identifies safe inheritance, autonomy attribution, and reliable verification as credibility problems. Our mechanism map relates these questions to retained history, component authority, and independent evaluation as supporting mechanisms, not proofs. Future critic evolution remains a proposal. Meta-Evolve does not claim any level merely from a deterministic fixture, and does not reproduce the survey’s reported results.

docs.title: AIDE²
docs.text: Weco's AIDE² report describes a bi-level experiment in which an outer autoresearch loop rewrites an inner research agent, evaluates each rewrite across heterogeneous tasks under a fixed cost, and selects using private scores. Its reported empirical claims belong to that system. Meta-Evolve's autoresearch teaching example demonstrates only the small nested-run, budget, evidence, and split boundaries; it is not a reproduction or evidence of recursive self-improvement.

docs.title: AlphaEvolve
docs.text: AlphaEvolve demonstrates coding-agent-driven evolutionary search for algorithmic and scientific problems. It is a reference for program artifacts, evaluator-guided evolution, and populations of executable candidates.

docs.title: FunSearch
docs.text: FunSearch combines LLM-generated programs with automated evaluation and evolutionary selection for mathematical discovery. It illustrates why executable artifacts and objective evaluators are powerful while also showing that the evaluator and representation bound the discovery process.

docs.title: OpenEvolve
docs.text: OpenEvolve is an open evolutionary coding-agent framework and useful implementation reference for program databases, evaluation, and search loops. Meta-Evolve should seek adapter compatibility where practical rather than duplicate APIs without benefit.

docs.title: EvoX
docs.text: EvoX motivates treating both solutions and the search strategy as evolving artifacts. This corresponds to nested task evaluation of PolicyArtifact and SearchProgram candidates.

docs.title: Group-Evolving Agents
docs.text: Group-Evolving Agents studies evolution at the level of composite agent groups and shared experience. It is relevant to TopologyArtifact, performance-novelty selection, and group-level mutation.

docs.title: Agent0 and Dr. Zero
docs.text: Agent0 and Dr. Zero explore proposer-solver co-evolution and self-generated curricula under verifiable rewards. They motivate explicit curriculum, checkpoint, training-job, and evaluator artifacts with separate validation boundaries.

docs.title: AERO
docs.text: AERO couples self-questioning, answering, criticism, and iterative model updates. It is relevant to synthetic-experience artifacts and external training loops consuming experience-graph views.

docs.title: CORAL
docs.text: CORAL is relevant to parallel coding agents, evaluated repository successors, shared knowledge, islands, and migration. In Meta-Evolve this becomes one GitTreeArtifact task configuration rather than the universal runtime model.

docs.title: Quality diversity and island models
docs.text: Quality-diversity methods, novelty search, MAP-Elites, Pareto archives, and island models are important baselines for maintaining heterogeneous strategies and avoiding premature convergence. They should be implemented as replaceable population and migration policies.

docs.title: MemGPT
docs.text: MemGPT frames agent memory as a hierarchy that moves information between limited context and external storage. Meta-Evolve's ContextPolicy operates at this transport boundary, while the experience graph defines durable causal search state beneath it.

docs.title: Graphiti and structured memory
docs.text: Graphiti is relevant to temporal knowledge graphs and dynamic synthesis of agent memory. Meta-Evolve additionally needs executable artifacts, objective rewards, search-policy state, training views, and causal sibling/path queries.

docs.title: Event sourcing and content addressing
docs.text:
Event sourcing, temporal databases, MVCC/change-data capture, content-addressed storage, reproducible build systems, and scientific provenance systems provide established foundations for immutable facts, current projections, time travel, lineage, deduplication, and audit.

Meta-Evolve should reuse conventional database and storage systems until its measured workload demonstrates a need for specialized physical design.

docs.title: Research questions for Meta-Evolve
docs.text:
• When does heterogeneous agent diversity improve compute-normalized progress?
  • Which context policies accelerate reuse without suppressing novelty?
  • Which topologies and migration policies avoid premature convergence?
  • How should compute be allocated among exploration, exploitation, repair, synthesis, and replication?
  • Which graph features predict the value of expanding or abandoning a branch?
  • How do skills and discoveries transfer across models, harnesses, tasks, and domains?
  • Which consistency guarantees are sufficient for concurrent search?
  • How should access changes and retractions propagate into derived skills, datasets, and checkpoints?
  • Can learned or evolved search policies generalize to held-out task distributions?
  • When do nested improvement loops plateau, destabilize, or exploit evaluators?
  • What evidence and replication policies predict real scientific validity?

docs.title: SealQA research labs
docs.text: Status: Experimental/live-only. These are small teaching mechanisms, not paper reproductions or an official SealQA evaluation. The complete curriculum contains at most 12 sessions.

docs.title: Where the notebooks are
docs.text: The two unexecuted notebooks live under examples/research/sealqa_labs/ and are published byte-for-byte under docs/notebooks/18_sealqa_research_labs/. Standalone chapters explain Feedback Descent and AutoData. Skill induction moved to the deterministic examples/research/context_evolution example.

docs.title: The common experimental substrate
docs.text: All labs consume a structural SessionRunner. The repository supplies orchestration and deterministic injected-runner tests; users supply any live SDK wrapper. The wrapper owns authentication, structured decoding, tools, permissions, model configuration, and provider telemetry.

docs.title: What is frozen and what may change
docs.text: The fixture questions, documents, evaluator-only answers, schemas, and session arithmetic are frozen. Candidate prompts and recipes may change. The wrapper declaration and all behavior-affecting configuration must be recorded before a live run.

docs.title: Leakage boundary
docs.text: Solver views contain only public document ids, titles, dates, and text. Gold answers, source URLs, split roles, evaluation rules, permissions, budgets, and promotion decisions remain outside candidate authority.

docs.title: Failure and scoring semantics
docs.text: Malformed structured output, missing candidates, timeout, exhaustion, SDK or infrastructure failure, and protected-control edits are typed and unrankable. They are never converted into a low score. Deterministic graders alone produce rankable measurements.

docs.title: Evidence, lineage, and identity
docs.text: Each session retains its label, decoded value or typed failure, wrapper evidence, token and elapsed usage, and experience counters. Derived artifacts name their source evidence. A wrapper configuration change changes declared identity and prevents uncontrolled comparison.

docs.title: How the shared components actually work
docs.text: UserSdkSessionRunner invokes a user-provided proposer inside an ordinary one-trial meta.run(). A successful wrapper returns ProposalResult, puts the schema-decoded value in sdk.structured-output evidence, and reports only shared token and elapsed usage. The lab validates that value again before using it.

docs.title: How to run the curriculum
docs.text:
Create an opt-in driver outside the shipped examples. Implement build_agent(request), identify its declaration, and pass it to UserSdkSessionRunner; then call run_selected. Review the maximum call count, SDK permissions, and spending limits before setting META_EVOLVE_LIVE_SDK=1.

No official provider capture is pending. Users may perform one authorized run with their own wrapper. Any published capture must identify the wrapper declaration and preserve ties, failures, null results, and regressions honestly. The notebooks contain illustrative code and no fabricated live output.

docs.title: Start here: improve a reusable prompt
docs.text:
You have a prompt that extracts action items from meeting notes, but its responses sometimes invent owners or miss unassigned work. Meta-Evolve tries revisions, evaluates their responses, and keeps the best measured prompt.

This first run uses handwritten model fixtures: fixed prompts and responses, with no credentials or live LLM calls. It teaches the loop, not model performance.

docs.title: See the problem
docs.text:
The starting prompt is “Extract action items from the meeting notes as JSON.” For the note below, its response invents an owner and deadline. The expected JSON keeps the task and uses null for both unknown fields; the revised response shown here matches that annotation.

From a checkout with Python 3.12+ and uv, install once with uv sync --locked. This command prints the incorrect extraction followed by a response matching the expected JSON:

uv run python examples/learn/meeting_notes/see_response.py
Output
Notes: We still need someone to check the pricing.
Seed response:
[
  {
    "task": "check the pricing",
    "owner": "Maya",
    "deadline": "Friday"
  }
]
Revised response:
[
  {
    "task": "check the pricing",
    "owner": null,
    "deadline": null
  }
]

docs.title: Run the improvement
docs.text:
uv run python examples/learn/meeting_notes/main.py
Output
Handwritten model fixtures; no live LLM calls.

Prompt          | Development cases passed
----------------|-------------------------
Starting prompt | 2/6
Revision 1      | 5/6 — selected
Revision 2      | 3/6

Selected prompt:
Extract agreed or explicitly needed action items as a JSON array. Use task phrases from the notes with fields task, owner, deadline. Use null for unstated owners or deadlines. Exclude unaccepted suggestions.

Usage: 2 revision attempts, 3 evaluations

Four-input excerpt from the complete executable source:

result = meta.improve(
    seed=SEED,
    proposer=rewrite_prompt,
    evaluator=evaluate_prompt,
    trials=2,
)

Read the four inputs in order:

  • seed=SEED is the initial extraction prompt, an ordinary Python string.
  • proposer=rewrite_prompt returns a replacement prompt from its parent.
  • evaluator=evaluate_prompt grades responses on six development cases.
  • trials=2 permits two revision attempts, after evaluating the seed.

docs.title: What produced those results?
docs.text:
The proposer wrapper calls the handwritten revisions. The evaluator wrapper calls the grader, which obtains fixture responses and compares their JSON with independent annotations. Scores are computed from responses, never assigned to prompt wording. Arbitrary prompt edits are unsupported by this fixture table and fail explicitly; a real model belongs at that boundary.

Each evaluation checks six notes: assigned work, unassigned work, missing deadlines, unaccepted suggestions, mixed notes, and a meeting with no actions. Three evaluations mean 18 case checks, not three model requests. The fixture reports zero model tokens because no model was called.

The starting prompt passes 2/6 cases, revision 1 passes 5/6, and revision 2 regresses to 3/6. Revision 1 still omits “verify the dashboard” in mixed notes; inspection shows the actual and expected JSON. Two revisions do not guarantee success, and the best prompt can precede the last.

The returned result is a Run, containing both the outcome and its history. result.best() returns an artifact view; .value is the full selected prompt printed above. The first proposer sees only its parent prompt. Evaluation failures are not automatically sent to it; the feedback lesson adds that path.

Development results guide selection. Three reserved final-check cases stay separate until after selection; they never guide another revision. Handwritten fixtures establish no generalization to new notes.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Copy examples/learn/meeting_notes/main.py to scratch_main.py beside it, so the sibling imports still resolve. Change trials=2 to trials=1. Run uv run python examples/learn/meeting_notes/scratch_main.py from the repository root. Predict the same 5/6 winner, one revision attempt, and two evaluations; revision 2 disappears from the table. Delete the scratch file. For a copy outside that directory, copy the whole directory, including its sibling modules, and run its main.py from the repository's uv environment.

Next: Define better

docs.title: Improve an agent’s skill library
docs.text:
After improving a single extraction prompt, change the documents an agent can consult. The candidate is now a skill library, while its quality is still measured through the behavior it produces. The fixture below keeps task evaluation independent of skill content; its two variants have different final-check boundaries, listed under “Who controls what.”

An agent needs a company-specific convention it cannot infer from its input. Treat the documents it reads as the candidate: a SkillSet containing one skills/<name>.md file per skill. The evaluator installs each candidate above an inner agent and measures its behavior on two tasks.

After uv sync --locked, run the offline fixture. It prints both the skill library and an optional itemized-playbook variant; it needs no SDK credentials.

uv run python examples/research/context_evolution/main.py
Output
== evoskill: skill documents ==
skills: ['skills/interest.md', 'skills/leases.md']
solved: 1.0
reported cost: 0 tokens, 0 spend_micros, 0.0 wall_seconds
outer kernel: 3 evaluations, 2 trials
wrapper calls: 6 of at most 6

== ace: context playbook ==
development solved: 0.0
lessons published: ['interest-element', 'lease-element']
items: ['interest-element', 'scale-in-thousands', 'lease-element']
active: ['interest-element', 'lease-element']
trial scores: ['0.0', '0.5', '1.0']
solved: 1.0
reported cost: 0 tokens, 0 spend_micros, 0.0 wall_seconds
outer kernel: 3 evaluations, 2 trials
wrapper calls: 14 of at most 14
consolidated: True (neutral) -> ['interest-element', 'lease-element']
held-out solved: 1.0

docs.title: Replace the fixture
docs.text:
Copy the context-evolution directory into a scratch directory to keep its sibling imports together. Start with the EvoSkill-inspired sibling (--sibling evoskill). Its skill_context.py declares evolve_skills(InnerAgent(...)): the declared agent owns a build(instructions) factory returning your ordinary SDK-backed proposer. Model, wrapper revision, and non-secret configuration identify the agent used inside evaluation.

Replace the two rollout tasks and their local checks with your development suite. Replace SKILL_LIBRARY and add_skill when you want a proposer that writes skills from failures. The current proposer picks missing documents from a fixed library using recorded randomness; it does not discover or write them. The inner fixture answers correctly only when its instructions contain the expected convention. Neither role uses a model in the default command.

docs.title: Who controls what
docs.text:
The candidate controls skill-document content. The evaluator controls task inputs, checks, and budgets. The outer search chooses among measured libraries; promotion remains external. An unfinished or unverifiable rollout is a typed failure, not a wrong answer scored zero.

Variant Data that influences selection Untouched evidence Skill documents Both evaluation episodes score every candidate None; private answers are hidden from the agent but scores guide search ACE playbook Published development lessons guide edits; private scores select; matched private checks decide consolidation A final held-out split, used after selection

The skill progression is zero, one-half, then one. It shows that the supplied conventions affect these two tasks. It does not reproduce EvoSkill’s discovery mechanism, benchmark gains, or cross-task transfer. The playbook’s held-out score has the same fixture-only limitation. Its development, consolidation, and held-out results live in memory; durable replay covers its outer search.

The fixture reports six skill-agent calls and fourteen playbook-agent calls, with zero reported provider cost. Use study.usage for the playbook’s complete cost, including phases outside search. A real wrapper must report actual usage.

For an exercise, remove one convention from a scratch copy’s skill library and predict which task can no longer improve. Restore it before trying your SDK.

Next: Improve an agent harness. For a separately addressable context representation, follow the canonical ACE notebook.

docs.title: Improve a prompt from evaluation feedback
docs.text:
Start with the meeting-notes tutorial. Its artifact is a reusable prompt; its evaluator measures the action-item responses that prompt produces. The parent prompt's failed development cases can guide a revision:

uv run python examples/learn/meeting_notes/prompt_feedback.py
Output
Without feedback: 5/6 development cases
With feedback: 6/6 development cases
Separate final check after selection: 3/3 reserved cases
Handwritten fixtures demonstrate separation, not generalization.

The candidate controls prompt text. The evaluator owns notes, annotations, checks, and the final-check split. AncestorsOnly pushes recorded development evidence; the rewriter keeps the latest failed cases. The three final cases are used only after selection. Handwritten response and rewrite fixtures demonstrate the mechanism, not model performance. Direct SDK replacement keeps the loop and grader while replacing the two model boundaries.

docs.title: Additional recipe: support-ticket routing
docs.text:
The existing ticket example offers a different integration shape: a user-owned agent edits files in an inner session. It is useful when your wrapper already operates on source trees. It is not required by the meeting-notes example.

A support-triage prompt omits the required reply format and the company’s routing rules. Run the deterministic example to produce a revised Text prompt, per-case scores, and a retained history. From a checkout, uv sync --locked is the only setup; no credentials or network are needed for this command.

uv run python examples/agents/prompt_optimization/main.py
Output
pass rate: 1.0
cases: {'double_charge': 1.0, 'login_error': 1.0, 'missing_feature': 1.0, 'refund_for_bug': 1.0}
session tokens: 0
evaluations: 2
--- winning prompt ---
Route duplicate charges to BILLING. Route login failures and refunds caused by product defects to PLATFORM. Route questions about unavailable features to SALES. Reply exactly as ROUTE: TEAM.

The seed scores zero and one revision passes all four cases. The evaluator runs an instructed agent on each ticket, then grades the answer with an exact local check. AncestorsOnly pushes recorded evaluation evidence; rewrite_prompt renders the failed cases into a workspace containing prompt.md and failing_cases.md. A user-owned agent edits the prompt, which becomes the next candidate. Search keeps the better measured prompt.

prompt → four ticket sessions → scores and failed replies
  ↑                                      ↓
new prompt ← rewrite session ← pushed evaluation evidence

docs.title: Replace the fixture
docs.text:
The canonical implementation owns the complete program. Copy that directory into a scratch directory before editing it; its sibling modules travel together.

  1. Replace fixture_agent(instructions) with your own SDK factory returning a source-tree proposer. Return ProposalResult when reporting token, spend, elapsed usage, or evidence. SDK integration shows this boundary; the SDK owns authentication and session lifecycle.
  2. Replace CASES and the checks in prompt_suite.py with your development tasks. Update EVAL_SUITE_VERSION when grading semantics change.
  3. Replace SEED_PROMPT and the rewrite instructions. Keep the evaluator and its answers outside candidate control.

The shipped rewriter is a fixed replacement containing all rules. It does not infer those rules from the feedback. The tests also drive a fake rewriter that uses the failure report in two steps. Both are deterministic stand-ins, not measurements of a model learning to write better prompts.

docs.title: What the evidence establishes
docs.text:
The candidate controls prompt text. The evaluator owns tickets, expected answers, grading, and session bounds. Search sees their feedback, so these are development cases, even though answers are absent from the seed prompt. There is no untouched validation split in this example. Add one before claiming performance beyond the four cases or making an external promotion decision.

Wrong replies are valid low scores. A missing reply makes evaluation fail; an unchanged rewrite is a proposer failure. Neither becomes a zero score. The captured session tokens: 0 is the fixture’s reported usage. The maximum is 14 wrapper sessions: three four-case evaluations plus two rewrites; the fixture stops after one rewrite and two evaluations.

For an exercise, copy the directory and remove one rule from the fixture’s replacement prompt. Predict which case scores change, then run the copy.

Next: Improve a skill library. The optional Feedback Descent research lab is Experimental/live-only and is separate from this deterministic recipe.

docs.title: From evaluated revisions to meta-evolution
docs.text: The meeting-notes tutorial starts with a familiar question: can a better prompt produce better extractions? These concepts explain the recorded process, independently of the model or artifact domain.

docs.title: What is being versioned?
docs.text:
The candidate is the prompt string. Each valid revision becomes a separately identified artifact occurrence, with its parent recorded. Generated action items are evaluation evidence in this example; they are not the artifact being searched. In another task, the response itself could be the artifact.

best().value gives you the selected prompt. lineage() shows the chain that produced it. Two attempts can produce identical prompt text yet remain distinct occurrences with their own parents, responses, and usage. See identity and artifact domains.

docs.title: What does evaluation establish?
docs.text:
The meeting-notes evaluator measures responses against its six development cases. Its score establishes fit to those cases, while the evidence lets you inspect missing tasks or invented owners. The evaluator stays independent of the candidate: a prompt cannot give itself a passing score or edit annotations.

A response with bad JSON fails an extraction check. A provider outage leaves no response to measure. These have different meanings and different recorded outcomes. See evidence, failures, and authority.

docs.title: How does search choose what to expand?
docs.text:
The proposer determines how a revision is made; search determines which parent receives an attempt and when to stop. Greedy expands the best measured prompt. BestOfN proposes independently from the seed. Neither makes every proposal an improvement. trials() retains unsuccessful attempts as well as the winner.

The search lesson holds the other components fixed while changing that choice. Search presets cover the other shipped strategies.

docs.title: What can a proposer learn from prior attempts?
docs.text: Recording evidence does not automatically expose it to the proposer. A context policy selects bounded prior records, or authorized pull access lets an agent request them. The meeting-notes feedback lesson sends the parent's failed development cases through the recorded context path. Final-check cases stay outside that path. See experience.

docs.title: What changes in meta-evolution?
docs.text:
First, hold the search strategy fixed and improve a prompt. Next, consider improving part of the procedure itself: the skill documents available to an agent, a permitted harness setting, or a search policy. An outer evaluation runs the candidate procedure and measures its inner results.

Level Candidate Evaluation Prompt improvement Extraction instructions Responses on notes Harness improvement Allowed harness surfaces Agent outcomes on task episodes Policy improvement Declared parent selection and trial limit Outcomes of inner improvement runs

The inner procedure's settings can be candidate content while the outer evaluation, budget, and promotion authority remain fixed. Shipped policy evolution uses trusted data-only artifacts, not arbitrary executable policies. These are relative inner and outer loops, not additional kernel types.

Follow nested evaluation, harness evolution, and policy evolution for runnable paths.

docs.title: What remains true across domains?
docs.text:
Evaluation, budgets, and permissions stay outside candidate authority. Selection does not deploy a result. Durable history preserves committed facts; it does not promise identical future external model responses. Budgets, durability, and conformance explain the details.

The architecture owns domain invariants and the programming model owns the shipped public API. Project status separates those capabilities from distributed and federated design proposals.

docs.title: Keep authority where it belongs
docs.text: A proposer can claim anything — a confident claim is not a measurement. Meta-Evolve survives unreliable proposers because every field in a run has exactly one owner. Start here demonstrates the separation; this page names it.

docs.title: Three fields, three owners
docs.text:
A trial's record splits into three kinds of fields:

  • Candidate-controlled — the proposed artifact content and its declared citations. Everything a proposer decides, and nothing else.
  • Experiment-controlled — the task, evaluator, hidden data, environment, seeds, and budgets. The evaluator scores independently; a proposer's claim about its own quality never moves a metric.
  • Governance-controlled — permissions, admission, visibility, and promotion. These live outside the run entirely.
candidate            experiment             governance
─────────            ──────────             ──────────
artifact content     evaluator + data       permissions
declared citations   budgets + seeds        visibility
                     environments           promotion

A candidate cannot read or edit the grader, enlarge its budget, erase a failure, or grant itself permissions. Those controls stay with the experiment and its operator.

Audited source inspection applies the same boundary to history: a proposer can receive only the bounded observations granted to it, while verification and presentation stay outside candidate authority. The full shipped boundary is owned by the M8.7 contract.

docs.title: Proposal is not promotion
docs.text:
Search may select a best measured artifact. That selection grants no production authority: promotion — actually deploying the selected artifact — is an external governance act that no candidate and no search policy can perform. A run ends with a recommendation and its evidence, never with a deployment. The harness- and policy-evolution examples print this boundary explicitly (promotion=external); see the harness evolution guide.

The authority invariants are canonical in the architecture and are not restated here.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Make a proposer attach a glowing self-assessment to its proposal metadata. Predict metrics identical to the same candidate without the self-praise: metadata is candidate-controlled, measurement is not.

Previous: Trust a shipped contract · Next: Fail with a type, not a zero

docs.title: Count the work exactly
docs.text:
The meeting-notes run evaluates the seed and two revisions, with six response calls per evaluation. usage() counts the three evaluations separately from model work reported by the wrapper. The supplemental minimal example below isolates the seed/attempt arithmetic.

uv run python examples/learn/checklist/_stories/search_story.py
Output
usage: Usage(evaluations=4, trials=3, tokens=0, spend_micros=0, wall_seconds=0.0)

docs.title: Five dimensions, one ledger
docs.text: Usage counts five dimensions: evaluations (each independent scoring), trials (each attempted successor), tokens (model usage a component reports), spend_micros (charged monetary spend a component reports, in integer micro-USD), and wall_seconds (recorded elapsed work). The transcript's arithmetic is exact: the seed costs one evaluation and no trial; each of three successors costs one trial and, when valid, one evaluation — four evaluations, three trials.

docs.title: Nobody widens their own budget
docs.text:
Budget is checked before more work starts, and exhaustion is a recorded stop reason, not an error. That preflight covers counts, tokens, and wall time; monetary spend is knowable only after a call returns, so it is enforced post-hoc — the action that crosses the ceiling fails typed and the run then admits no further work at all, free work included, because the halt is recorded against the run rather than against the next action's price. A candidate or component never grants itself additional work; the run budget can narrow what a search preset would attempt, never expand it.

Spend is adjudicated at two scopes, and the second is not derivable from the first: the aggregate remainder, and each trial's own declared ceiling. A policy may submit per-trial ceilings while the task leaves spend unbounded, in which case the aggregate rule never arms and only the per-trial one stops paid work. Both are folds over committed facts, so live, resumed, and replayed runs reach the same verdict.

docs.title: Experience has its own meter
docs.text:
uv run python examples/learn/experience_reuse/learning_story.py
Output
pushed context: (10, 3)
audited pull: (10, 7, 20)

Memory reads are charged outside the task ledger, on their own separate bounds. The transcript pairs each score with its memory bill: pushed context reports (score, records pushed) and audited pull reports (score, operations, records returned). A proposer reading history spends experience budget, never evaluation budget, so memory can neither starve nor subsidize the search itself. run.experience_usage() exposes the meter on any result.

Exact-source inspection and its optional Git presentation use that same separate experience account. The canonical operation and charging rules stay with the M8.7 contract and the programming model.

Accounting rules are canonical in the architecture and the evaluation and budgets guide, and are not restated here.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Change max_trials=3 to max_trials=2 in the first transcript's Greedy run. Predict Usage(evaluations=3, trials=2, ...): one fewer attempted successor, one fewer independent scoring, and nothing else moves.

Previous: Fail with a type, not a zero · Next: Encode any artifact

docs.title: Trust a shipped contract
docs.text: You wrote a custom evaluator, codec, or search program. How do you know it obeys the same rules the built-in components obey? You run the same published tests the library runs on itself.

docs.title: What a conformance suite is
docs.text:
meta_evolve.conformance publishes one pytest-native suite per extension component family. Each suite is a plain class of laws whose collaborators arrive as fixtures: subclass it, name the subclass Test... so pytest collects it, override the fixtures with your component, and the laws run against your implementation.

published suite               your test module
───────────────               ────────────────
ArtifactCodecTests      <--   class TestMyCodec(ArtifactCodecTests):
  law: decode(encode(v))          fixture: my codec
  law: decode is validation       fixture: rejected payloads
  law: no aliasing                fixture: mutable values

The suites install through an explicit extra, so using the library never pulls in a test runner:

uv sync --extra conformance

docs.title: What the library proves about itself
docs.text:
Every published suite is subclassed inside the repository's own tests, so the built-in codecs, evaluators, policies, and search programs pass exactly the laws an extension author receives. A suite also states what it does not check as carefully as what it does: EvaluatorTests skips its typed-failure law, visibly, when a subclass declares no rejected candidates, and ArtifactCodecTests does the same for its aliasing law. Silence is never counted as passing.

One law is easy to think redundant and is not: EvaluatorTests checks that scoring does not edit the candidate. With built-in codecs an evaluator only ever sees a frozen decoded value — but a custom codec that returns the instance it was handed gives the evaluator the real thing, so the law waits where the damage would land.

docs.title: When you reach for one
docs.text:
• You registered an artifact domain — run your codec through ArtifactCodecTests, as Add an artifact domain does in its final step.
  • You wrote an evaluator, context policy, workspace, sandbox, search program, or repository proposer — the operations lab lists every family and its published suite.

Suite contents and deliberate limitations are canonical in the extensions guide and are not restated here.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Subclass ArtifactCodecTests around a codec whose decode returns the exact instance it was handed, and declare one mutable value. Predict a named aliasing-law failure, not a vague error: the suite tells you which contract your codec broke.

Previous: Attach evidence to results · Next: Keep authority where it belongs

docs.title: Encode any artifact
docs.text:
The first prompt example uses an ordinary Python string through the default python-value artifact contract. You do not need to declare a new domain for it. Explicit text, source, and skill domains become useful when their distinct representation or mutation contracts matter.

The loop never inspects what it improves. A number, a prompt, a repository, a harness — every artifact travels as a typed payload that one registered codec translates, so no coordinator code branches on what you evolve.

docs.title: Six built-in kinds
docs.text:
Every artifact is stored under a (kind, representation) key. Six keys ship built in:

Kind Representation What it holds python-value canonical-json any canonically serializable value — the default text utf8-text-v1 one UTF-8 document: a prompt, a config, an essay source-tree utf8-tree-v1 an immutable directory of UTF-8 files skill-set utf8-tree-v1 named skill documents agent-harness harness-manifest-v1 a portable agent-harness bundle search-policy policy-manifest-v1 declarative search-policy values

Text optimization and context evolution run two of these through the identical meta.run call site; SQL migrations registers a seventh, custom domain and is the runnable tour of everything on this page.

docs.title: Kind versus representation
docs.text: The kind, never the bytes, decides which codec reads a committed payload. source-tree and skill-set share the same tree bytes (utf8-tree-v1) and still decode differently, because a payload's meaning is a declared contract rather than an inference from its shape.

docs.title: Why custom domains stay durable-local
docs.text:
A registered custom codec is a live Python object with no verifiable manifest. A durable run must be reopenable by a reader who can decode every payload from the record alone — a payload another machine cannot decode is not shareable evidence. So durable-local mode accepts only the six built-in keys and rejects a custom codec before writing any event, with no silent fallback. A local run with a custom domain still works and may still write durable storage; reopening it later means rebuilding the same registry in Python, which grants decoding, not resumption.

To build a domain end to end, follow Add an artifact domain. Codec laws are canonical in the programming model and the published conformance suite, and are not restated here.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Seed a text task with a tuple instead of a string. Predict a typed refusal at ingress — utf8-text-v1 tasks require a str value — before any trial runs: decode and encode are validation, not best-effort coercion.

Previous: Count the work exactly · Build one: Add an artifact domain

docs.title: Attach evidence to results
docs.text:
In the meeting-notes tutorial, a 5/6 score does not reveal which task was missed. The selected attempt's evidence contains the actual response, annotation, and failed check for the mixed notes. The supplemental program below explores who can publish and read such records.

A score says how good a candidate measured. Evidence says what was actually observed on the way to that measurement — and who observed it. Three different authorities can attach evidence to one run, and they never blur.

uv run python examples/learn/experience_reuse/evidence_story.py
Output
seed evidence: ('grader-transcript',)
successor evidence: ('hypothesis-note', 'grader-transcript')
last proposal derived from: 3 prior records
audited pull: operations=6 records=8

docs.title: 1. Evidence on an evaluation
docs.text: The evaluator returns an EvaluationResult that carries an EvidenceDraft beside its metrics. The seed trial shows only grader-transcript: evaluator-authored evidence of what the grader observed. Evidence records what was observed; it is not a candidate-controlled score.

docs.title: 2. Evidence on a proposal
docs.text: The proposer returns a ProposalResult with a draft of its own. The successor trial adds hypothesis-note: candidate-authored evidence stating the claim behind the change. A proposer can write anything here, and its score does not move — the metrics stay with the independent evaluator.

docs.title: 3. Evidence a later candidate can read
docs.text:
With PullAccess, a later proposal searches prior evidence records and opens the ones it uses. The last proposal cited three: the seed's grader transcript plus both records from the first successor. Every read is audited — six operations and eight returned records are charged and inspectable — and the citations land in the trial's derived_from edges.

This page is about evidence records inside a run. The Evidence notebooks navigation section is different: it holds the captured notebook companions to the Learn chapters.

Evidence fields and authority are canonical in the programming model and architecture and are not restated here.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Remove the hypothesis-note draft from the proposer. Predict the successor line shrinking to ('grader-transcript',) while derived_from still cites two prior records: the proposal's citations never depended on the proposal publishing evidence of its own.

Previous: Tell equal bytes apart · Next: Trust a shipped contract

docs.title: Fail with a type, not a zero
docs.text:
In the meeting-notes lesson, a completed response with invalid JSON fails the extraction check: the prompt is a valid candidate whose behavior was measured. An unavailable model leaves nothing to measure. The latter is a typed failure with no score. The supplemental example below isolates a malformed candidate proposal, which is also non-rankable.

uv run python examples/learn/checklist/_stories/search_story.py
Output
failure: ('trial_failed', 'InvalidOutput')

A proposer that returns an unusable object produces a failed trial with a named type. The run records what went wrong instead of inventing a number.

docs.title: The failure kinds
docs.text: Invalid candidate shape, proposer failure, evaluator failure, timeout, resource exhaustion, policy violation, and infrastructure failure all retain distinct types and details. The distinctions matter because the correct responses differ: retry a flaky environment, fix a broken proposer, and never penalize a candidate for the grader's crash.

docs.title: Rankable or non-rankable, never fake
docs.text: A trial with a valid independent evaluation is rankable: search may select it. A trial without one is non-rankable: it never becomes zero, negative infinity, or a fabricated metric, so no failure can outrank or sandbag an honestly measured candidate.

docs.title: Two failures that look alike but are not
docs.text:
uv run python examples/domains/python_function/learning_story.py
Output
invalid proposal: InvalidOutput
evaluator failure: EvaluatorFailure

Improve source runs three negative cases: a poor candidate is valid, evaluated, and rankable at 0.0; a patch whose expected bytes do not match is InvalidOutput with no successor; a broken grader is EvaluatorFailure with no score at all. The agent test-repair and adversarial-inputs examples push the same boundary further: three outcomes, not two.

Failure semantics are canonical in the architecture and are not restated here.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Make the failing proposer in the first transcript return a well-formed tuple instead. Predict the trial_failed line becoming an evaluated trial: the type disappears because the cause disappeared, not because a score was substituted.

Previous: Keep authority where it belongs · Next: Count the work exactly

docs.title: Tell equal bytes apart
docs.text:
In prompt search, two independent rewrites can return the same instructions. They still represent two attempts with separate responses and usage. The tiny identity-only example below isolates that rule.

A proposer can hand back a value byte-identical to one the run has already seen. Are they the same artifact? Meta-Evolve answers with two identities: one for the bytes, one for the causal event that produced them.

uv run python examples/learn/checklist/_stories/identity_story.py
Output
seed: id=f953e1f8 digest=6ae048f0 parents=()
successor: id=227a6a34 digest=6ae048f0 parents=('f953e1f8',)
successor: id=99877b49 digest=6ae048f0 parents=('f953e1f8',)
content digests equal: True
distinct occurrence ids: 3

The proposer restates its parent unchanged, twice, under BestOfN. Three artifacts hold the same five bytes. The run still records three distinct things.

docs.title: Content identity is the bytes
docs.text: The digest is a stable hash of the encoded artifact value. All three rows share 6ae048f0 because all three values are "draft". Equal bytes always produce an equal digest, so storage deduplicates payloads and a transcript of digests stays stable across reruns. The lineage: ('659bfe4a', '08abe248') line in Improve source prints exactly this: a digest prefix for each lineage step.

docs.title: Occurrence identity is the causal event
docs.text:
The occurrence id names one appearance of those bytes at one position in the run: proposed from which parents, at which logical step. The seed has no parents. Each successor names the seed as its parent and receives its own id. Equal artifact bytes in different causal positions remain different occurrences.

This distinction is also why audited source inspection authorizes an exact prior occurrence rather than matching content alone. The shipped contract and its storage edge are owned by M8.7.2–M8.7.3.

docs.title: Why the run needs both
docs.text:
Two trials that produce byte-identical artifacts remain different causal events: they may have different parents, observations, usage, and failures. Collapsing them would erase which attempt actually earned its evaluation. Replay and audited experience address records by causal position, never by content, so history stays exact even when values repeat. The experience lesson shows the same rule inside the temporal graph.

Both identities are canonical in the architecture and are not restated here.

docs.title: Change and predict
docs.text:
Change restate to return parent + "!". Predict digests that stop being equal while the parent links stay exactly the same: content identity follows the bytes; occurrence identity never depended on them.

Back to Learn · Next: Attach evidence to results

docs.title: A4.4 auditable proposal contract design brief
docs.text:
Status: Design—not shipped. This retained decision brief records the design that preceded the A4.4 slice of harness evolution. Current executable semantics live in examples/research/harness_evolution/ and the tests that pin it; the slice's requirements and acceptance criteria live in its tracking issue.

Require every harness proposal to carry a falsifiable, auditable mutation manifest; refuse an incomplete or unauthorized one with a typed unrankable outcome; and let the opt-in live driver speak the same contract without disturbing its historical capture. The primary inspiration is AHE's third pillar — decision observability — translated in the reference notes rather than reproduced.

docs.title: One wire contract, two responders
docs.text:
The deterministic fixture and the live SDK exchange one closed object, harness-proposal-manifest/v1: the authorized observations the edit rests on, the single surface and value it changes, the development behavior it predicts will improve, and the regressions it puts at risk. Every field is required, so an edit that cannot say what it expects is not an edit this example ranks. additionalProperties is false at every object level, and the singular surface field is the only mutation target.

The provider schema and the trusted decoder are deliberately not the same authority. A schema is sent to a service that may or may not honor it, so its surface enum is a convenience for the model while the parent's own declaration is the allowlist — and only the caller holds the parent. The decoder therefore compares decoded keys against its own field tuple, never raises, and authorizes the surface last.

Two array rules cannot live in the schema at all: the Structured Outputs subset lists no uniqueItems and cannot express element order. They are decoder-only rules, and the prompt states both — a live model refused for a constraint it was never told would be a refusal about the prompt rather than about the proposal.

docs.title: Citations are positional tokens over an ordered ledger
docs.text:
Diagnosis citations are record-granular. The adapter builds its ledger from the exact ContextBundle.records it validated, in committed order, and assigns e0, e1, … Diagnosis evidence, evaluations, and trial outcomes stay distinct rather than collapsing behind an evaluation reference, so a later proposal can cite the failure it was shown.

The model sees only a token and a model-safe presentation of the record, and returns tokens; the trusted side resolves them back to the references it put in. A fabricated identity cannot become a derivation, and a real one the model was never shown cannot either. Resolved citations become ProposalResult.derived_from; the model never emits a serialized ExperienceRef. Order is required rather than merely recorded, because the resolved tuple is committed — requiring the ledger's own order leaves the model choosing only the subset.

citation_ledger is kept empty of domain knowledge: it assigns tokens, resolves them totally, and admits occurrences, while its caller decides what is citable and how to describe it safely. That is what lets a later slice append a second observation channel without changing it.

docs.title: Position is the kernel's, not the ledger's
docs.text:
Proposal completion accepts derived_from only as an ordered unique subsequence of the observations a run committed: the pushed selection, then each succeeded pull result in operation order, deduplicated by first observation. A reference's canonical position is therefore fixed by the operation that first exposed it, not by the order a caller opened it. A ledger appending in open order can disagree — one search exposing two references, opened in reverse, resolves perfectly in the adapter and is then discarded under a policy violation whose details name nothing, because the proposal reported no failure of its own.

So Ledger carries an exposure tuple recording what each of the caller's own operations returned, in the order it returned them, deduplicated by first observation exactly as the kernel's ledger is. An occurrence already citable takes no pull position: a search may return a reference the pushed selection already put in the ledger, and the kernel observed that one ahead of every pull result. Admission then refuses, before the read, an occurrence no recorded observation exposed and one exposed before an occurrence already citable. Nothing recorded in exposure is citable — only a completed open is — so it asserts no provenance; it states what the caller's own operation exposed.

Alternatives rejected:

  • Reordering entries to first-observed position cannot be done in general: the ledger has no position for an unexposed reference, and repairing afterwards would already have spent the open a refusal costs nothing to prevent.
  • Deriving order from a record's event_sequence is wrong rather than weaker — a later search can expose an older record, and the kernel keeps operation order, not commit order.
  • Having the admission boundary perform the search too would put filters and limits, a domain choice, inside a module deliberately empty of them.

docs.title: Admission performs the read
docs.text: Only a completed open is citable, and no inspection of a value can enforce that: a one-result search returns exactly what an open does, and the kernel authorizes searched references too, so a searched occurrence admitted by mistake would meet no later refusal anywhere. A caller passing in an observation plus a label describing how it got it would be asserting provenance rather than establishing it. The boundary therefore opens the reference itself, and there is no parameter through which anything else can arrive. A truncated open is refused, because a partial view is still a view the model would cite as whole. Owning the read also means the entry's presentation is derived from the record that read returned, so a caller whose presentation is the content it cites needs no second open.

docs.title: The projection owns diagnosis lineage
docs.text: diagnosis_reading remains the sole owner of diagnosis ownership and validity, and its Attempt projection retains the diagnosis reference alongside its decoded payload and evaluation reference. The adapter does not re-scan bundle records: once the parent's own evaluated attempt is selected — by digest, not by recency, since the bundle also carries rejected siblings — the parent's two tokens are resolved through the ledger. Both references came from the same validated bundle that built the ledger, so a missing token is an internal invariant violation rather than a new typed refusal.

docs.title: Refusal and retention
docs.text:
Refusal is staged, because it is not all-or-nothing. Citations resolve first and survive a later invalid field; a complete manifest survives a typed mutation failure; what a stage never established is never invented. An incomplete manifest retains the bounded raw response — the only record of what the model said, bounded so a refusal cannot cost more storage than a success — as proposer evidence the governed policy never selects.

Every refusal message is a constant. A typed failure is committed to the trial outcome and the governed policy selects outcome records whole, so a message quoting the offending value would hand the next proposal the text the refusal exists to reject. For the same reason a mutation on an undeclared surface is refused by the parent-derived pre-check before apply(), whose typed failure would otherwise echo the model's chosen surface string into a selectable record.

One exception crosses the boundary: Ledger raises DuplicateCitation, its own ValueError subclass, and the adapter catches that type alone. Only a duplicated reference is a fact about the bundle it was handed; any other ValueError out of building or rendering a ledger is a bug in the example, and retaining it as an unreadable bundle would commit a diagnosis of the wrong thing.

docs.title: Types where comments used to be
docs.text:
Three seams were typed as object and asserted in prose. A request_field(request, key, kind) reader lives beside the responder contract, because a responder is handed the opaque mapping a provider would receive and a wrong type there is a bug in whoever built the request, so it raises. The retention keywords are a TypedDict, so the splat into ProposalResult is checked rather than passed as an untyped mapping. A mapping manifest value becomes a FrozenMap at the mutation boundary, which is what the mutation's own constructor would make of it.

The decoder checks and keeps each field in one place for the same reason: a value narrowed in one function and constructed in another can only be asserted, and an assertion a type checker cannot see is not narrowing.

docs.title: Live driver
docs.text:
The driver names the one shared schema rather than restating it — a second copy would be a second contract the moment either side moved — and decodes nothing itself. Parsing, citation resolution, surface authorization, mutation, and retention all belong to the shared adapter, so a live run and a fixture run differ only in who answers. The driver's prompt is rendered from the adapter's sanitized request alone, and the suite executes it against one real governed handoff so a request-key rename fails before an authorized paid call.

The historical capture stays byte-identical and is pinned by an exact SHA-256 assertion. A future authorized keyword-compatibility rejection is the retained result of that run, not permission to rerun it.

docs.title: Boundaries this slice keeps
docs.text:
HarnessMutation, ProposalResult, and Proposal are not widened: surface and value lower onto the existing singular mutation, and predictions and risks are retained under existing fields. Private and held-out facts never enter pushed context, pull experience, prompts, or derivation. Matched private selection and the final output repin belong to the next slice, so development search, held-out comparison, export, durability, accounting, and external promotion are preserved unchanged here.

Three properties remain Meta-Evolve's stricter translation rather than paper requirements, labelled as such in the reference notes: exact authorized citations through derived_from, exactly one declared surface per proposal, and a typed refusal when the contract is incomplete.

docs.title: A4.2 evaluator-owned source views design brief
docs.text:
Status: Design—not shipped. This retained decision brief records the design that preceded the A4.2 slice of harness evolution. Current executable semantics live in examples/research/harness_evolution/ and the tests that pin it; the slice's requirements and acceptance criteria live in its tracking issue.

Give a harness proposer the complete mutable surface values of prior candidates without giving it a filesystem. The primary inspiration is Meta-Harness's agent-directed inspection of prior candidates, translated in the reference notes rather than reproduced: there, an agent browses a directory; here, a fixed evaluator publishes a value and a trusted adapter retrieves it through the shipped audited reader.

docs.title: A view is a value, and its owner is the evaluation
docs.text:
The evaluator is the only thing holding the evaluated artifact under its own authority, so it is the only thing that may publish a view of it. What it publishes is three files — manifest.json, surfaces/planner.md, surfaces/context_policy.json — as a SourceTree value carried in evidence. No artifact is minted. Nothing enters lineage, selection, export, or promotion.

That layout is deliberately not the one harness/export.py writes. Export is the egress contract for a selected harness: flat, indented for a human, and carrying the artifact id and digest it came from. Those identities are exactly what an evidence value must not carry, and a format free to evolve for human readers is exactly what a wire schema must not be pinned to. Two contracts over the same two surfaces, kept apart on purpose.

docs.title: The bundle is atomic, or it is a stated absence
docs.text:
A development evaluation emits a harness-source-index/v1 header at offset 0, then one harness-source-file/v1 per indexed path, then the raw capture and the governed diagnosis. Construction runs before any episode: a view that cannot be built costs no episode work and never becomes a low score. There is no partial tuple and no code for one, because there is no way to reach it.

When construction fails the evaluation emits a harness-source-error/v1 header instead — split, the shipped artifact digest, and one of three fixed codes, with no path, no partial digest list, no content, and no rejected value. It also retains an incomplete diagnosis, because the A4.1 bundle reader treats an evaluated attempt carrying no diagnosis as corruption of the whole bundle and would otherwise refuse every later proposal in the run over one failed view.

Offsets are navigation inside one owned bundle, never durable identity. Evaluation.evidence_ids[offset] owns each occurrence, and the index says which offsets are source files — which is what keeps the raw episode capture unreachable through this channel even though it sits in the same bundle.

docs.title: Admission is conditional, because a token cannot be withdrawn
docs.text:
The A4.4 admission rule performs the read and builds the citation entry before a caller can check that the payload is one of the two kinds this channel authorizes. So the ledger it returns is a candidate: the caller validates the record it opened and then adopts that ledger or keeps the one it had. Discarding is order-safe — a non-adopted reference stays exposed, is never counted among the admitted, and blocks no later admission.

Adopting first and repairing afterwards would not do. A token, once assigned, is what the model is shown, and there is no way to take it back out of a prompt that has already been built. Discarding the admission does not discard the exposure, though: the open really happened and took a position in the kernel's own pull order, and the caller's record of that order stays true whether or not it goes on to cite what came back.

Validating the payload is not enough on its own. The outer evidence kind and the payload are both things a candidate can influence, so both are checked, and they are checked against each other — otherwise a record whose data happens to look like an index enters the allowlist under whatever kind it likes, including the raw capture's.

Exactly one condition is an absence: a valid error header, which is the evaluator successfully saying no view exists there. Everything else refuses — including an evaluation carrying no evidence at all, which is a broken run rather than a quiet gap, and which three independent gates close on.

docs.title: The budget is a bound, not headroom
docs.text:
One search plus four opens per prior evaluation. At the flagship's second proposal that is nine operations, ten results, and ten records against a declared ten, ten, and ten — the caps are reached exactly, with one operation slot spare, and a third proposal fails closed rather than widening a limit.

Encodability is decided before any byte length or digest, because both begin with the same encode. A lone surrogate cannot become UTF-8, and a validator that raises on it is not a validator — the producer never emits one, which is the reason only a hostile payload reaches that check.

Nesting is bounded too, and separately, because a byte count does not catch it: roughly 1,800 bytes of nested arrays sits under every size limit and still exhausts the stack in parsing, in the canonical re-encode, and in freezing. The bound is enforced on both sides — the producer refuses to publish a view its own reader would reject — and the reader keeps a recursion guard behind it so the refusal does not depend on the interpreter's limit.

The character cap is measured against what the schemas permit rather than what the flagship spends. Canonical serialization expands a control character roughly six-fold, so two complete 40 KiB views of adversarial-yet-legal surface values render to about 500,000 characters against a declared 512,000. Crossing it truncates an open, which is refused, so the failure is closed and typed — never a leak and never a low score. The arithmetic is derived from the declared limits in a test, so raising a limit or indexing another file fails loudly instead of silently overflowing a live run.

docs.title: Identity has to cover the code, not only the constants
docs.text:
The fixed registry records what a component reaches as a dependency closure and hashes the modules, so splitting or editing a source module moves the proposer's version. A live component has no registry behind it: configured_local hashes a version string and nothing else. Declaring the schemas, renderer, paths, limits, and granted access is therefore not enough — all of that can hold still while the code reading through it changes.

So the same closure is declared for the live path and hashed by the same shipped helper. Its own proposer is a closure over the SDK client, which implementation_digest refuses by design, so the digest is taken over the module-level adapter that closure delegates to and the modules it reads through.

The driver's own module is in that closure too. Rendering the prompt and reading the SDK response are as much the proposer's behaviour as the trusted adapter is, and neither shows up in a schema or a limit. The live evaluator gets the same treatment for the same reason: its suite digest, budget, timeouts, and published channels can all hold still while its code changes.

docs.title: What this is not
docs.text: It is not a filesystem, a Git history, or a generic source-view seam. The shipped list_source_paths, read_source, and diff_source operations are not widened to accept a harness artifact, and the local parent/prior comparison the prompt carries is example-owned rendering over two values the adapter already holds rather than an audited diff operation. It is a Meta-Harness-inspired evaluator-owned mechanism retrieved through Meta-Evolve's audited experience reader, not a reproduction of that paper's system, benchmarks, or reported gains.

docs.title: M10 local-author design
docs.text:
Status: Design—not shipped.

This page is the subordinate design record for #151 (M10.0). The milestone roadmap owns status, order, gates, and exclusions. The implementation plan owns technical staging. Journey 2's Experiment declaration and dual-form run() call are shipped by M10.1, Journey 1's improve() call is shipped by M10.2, Journey 3's functional search is shipped by M10.3, and the aggregate Run.inspect() read model is shipped by M10.4. Journey 4's Session is shipped by M10.6. The read-only local browser shipped in M10.7; frozen-payload artifact presentation, previews, diffs, and canonical attachments shipped in M10.8. At the time of this record the parent M10 remained open. Its current status is owned by the milestone roadmap.

The live examples were later reorganized by user journey under examples/learn/, domains/, operations/, agents/, and research/. Numbered paths below are frozen historical measurement evidence; the live functional-search fixtures now reside at examples/learn/functional_search/, and the live future reservation is examples/research/trusted_workers/.

The public story is: proposers create candidates, evaluators judge them, search decides what to try next, and Meta-Evolve records the entire process.

docs.title: Vocabulary tiers
docs.text:
The beginner tier names the seed, proposer, evaluator, and bounded trials=. The declarative tier adds Task, Experiment, search, context, experience, random seed, and registry. Storage, execution mode, and a narrowing budget are execution overlays. The extension tier retains SearchProgram.next() and the kernel records needed by advanced policy authors.

trials= is an author-facing cost and control limit, not exposure of kernel Trial records. Search state, trial specifications, operators, work items, events, and raw randomness stay off the simple path.

docs.title: Measurement rules
docs.text:
A physical line is every nonblank, non-comment code line. Imports and lines containing only delimiters count. Every counted line is classified once: algorithm expresses the limit, selection, stopping, or domain declaration; scaffolding adapts protocols, identities, execution, or syntax around those choices. Proposer, evaluator, and artifact-domain logic is held outside every search slice.

The shipped before-side for functional search is this runnable full-protocol shape, reduced from the repository's custom-search test without changing its protocol work:
